# Paper Framing — gen-depth-fingerprint

## Target Venue
- **Primary: EMNLP 2026 ARR (deadline: May 25, 2026)** — D012
- Fallback: ICLR 2027 (Sep 24), NAACL 2027 ARR (Oct 16)

## Core Insight
Non-paraphrastic LLM generation chains exhibit **differential depth response**: **central-tendency/diversity features** (entropy_mean, TTR, hapax ratio) drift monotonically with depth, while **distributional shape features** (entropy_std, tail_decay) remain near-stationary. This differential response is consistent with recursive generation inducing a **location shift** in the NLL distribution — the text becomes progressively more predictable (mean shifts) while the functional form of the distribution is preserved (shape is invariant). The genuine novelty is not the drift/stationarity split per se (which follows from location-shift properties), but: (a) the **task formulation** (ordinal depth estimation beyond binary detection), (b) **empirical validation** across 6 generators / 3 model families (including 7B+ scale) showing this pattern is robust, (c) the practical consequence that combining both feature types yields **complementary signal** for depth classification. **Primary metric (D017)**: binary LOGO F1 = 0.723 (gen-1 vs gen-2+, excluding gen-0 due to shared-seed leakage). 3-class LOGO F1 = 0.789 reported as supplementary with gen-0 caveat. Per-generator held-out F1: 0.68–0.86 (std=0.058). Key finding: in binary evaluation (no gen-0 leakage), 7-feature (0.723) > 4-baseline ensemble (0.712) — baseline advantage in 3-class was entirely from gen-0 classification. Depth signal is scale-invariant as a phenomenon, though cross-scale classifier transfer shows a moderate gap (8B held-out F1=0.69 vs ≤2.8B 0.76-0.85).

## Core Claims (3 条，均可证伪)

**Claim 1 — Depth Discriminability**: Distributional features computed under a held-out reference model can classify text generation depth with F1 significantly above chance, generalizing across unseen generators (leave-one-generator-out evaluation). Primary metric: binary LOGO F1 = 0.723 (gen-1 vs gen-2+, gen-0 excluded due to shared-seed overlap). 3-class (gen-0/gen-1/gen-2+) LOGO F1 = 0.789 supplementary with caveat.

**Claim 2 — Differential Depth Response & Feature Complementarity**: Depth-dependent features exhibit differential response: central-tendency/diversity features (entropy_mean, TTR, hapax_ratio) drift monotonically with depth (consistent with location shift in NLL distribution), while shape features (entropy_std, tail_decay) remain near-stationary. In binary eval, 7-feature ensemble (0.723) outperforms 4-baseline detector ensemble (0.712) by +1.1pp and all individual detectors (+1.1–19.9pp). The 4-baseline advantage in 3-class (0.796 vs 0.789) is entirely from gen-0 classification. Ordinal-specific methods (CORAL 0.771, Frank-Hall 0.793) do not outperform XGBoost (0.789) — CI overlap at 3-class granularity.

**Claim 3 — Downstream Utility (Negative Finding)**: Depth-aware data curation does NOT improve downstream CLM quality compared to random subsampling. At equal data count, size_matched (random control, ppl=2.367) outperforms depth01 (depth-stratified, 2.387) and binary_filtered (2.389). The primary determinant is data quantity, not depth composition (all 12K samples → ppl=2.335). Depth fingerprinting is an effective **diagnostic** tool for characterizing provenance, but not a **curative** tool for data curation. This honest negative finding is reported transparently.

## Story Spine

**Problem**: Web-scraped training data increasingly contains LLM-generated text of unknown provenance depth. Current detection methods offer only binary real-vs-synthetic classification, forcing all-or-nothing filtering: discard everything flagged as synthetic (losing useful gen-1 content) or keep everything (admitting high-risk deep-generation text with compounding distributional drift).

**Existing approaches & gaps**: Binary detectors (FastDetectGPT, SynthID-Text, LD-Score) cannot distinguish gen-1 from gen-2+. Attractor cycle theory (ACL 2025) proves paraphrasing chains converge to 2-period cycles, bounding depth signal to ~3 classes — but this result depends on the semantic-preservation constraint of paraphrasing. No existing work attempts generation depth estimation. When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, single detector scores (Avg-LogProb 0.737, LD-Score 0.655, FastDetectGPT 0.688, Binoculars 0.417 under 6-gen LOGO) show moderate signal but **high per-generator F1 variance** (e.g., AvgLogProb range 0.615–0.805, 19.0pp span), making them unreliable as standalone depth estimators.

**Our framing**: We characterize distributional drift in recursive non-paraphrastic LLM generation, revealing **differential depth response**: level/diversity features (including reference-model entropy_mean) drift monotonically with depth, while distributional shape features (entropy variance, tail decay) remain near-stationary. This split is about **what the feature measures** (central tendency vs shape), not where it comes from. The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that **significantly and consistently** outperforms all single-detector baselines: binary LOGO F1 = 0.723 (gen-1 vs gen-2+, p<0.001 vs Avg-LogProb 0.712, LD-Score 0.701, FastDetectGPT 0.616, Binoculars 0.524). In the leak-free binary evaluation, 7-feature (0.723) > 4-baseline ensemble (0.712), reversing the 3-class result where baseline advantage came entirely from gen-0 classification. The practical advantage is **reliability across unknown generators** — per-generator F1 std = 0.058 for our ensemble vs higher variance for individual detectors.

**Headline result template**: "On non-paraphrastic continuation chains across 6 base-model generators from 3 model families (0.6B–8.2B), our 7-feature distributional ensemble achieves binary LOGO F1 of 0.72 for leak-free depth discrimination (gen-1 vs gen-2+), outperforming all individual detection baselines. Per-generator held-out F1 ranges from 0.68 to 0.86 (std=0.051). Depth-aware data curation does not outperform random subsampling for downstream CLM quality, establishing depth fingerprinting as a diagnostic tool for provenance characterization, not a curative tool for data selection."

## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns

**RC1 — "Is this just vocabulary impoverishment?"**: Surface features alone achieve 0.73 macro-F1, but full 7-feature ensemble achieves 0.789 3-class / 0.723 binary (p<0.001). We don't claim reference features are "better" — we show they capture a **different, complementary** signal (stationary distributional shape vs drifting level/diversity). Note: "fingerprint" in the paper refers to the full feature vector's combination, not just reference-model features.

**RC7 — Pre-registered prediction (LD-Score)**: LD-Score (character-distribution signature) measures character-level distributional properties. We predict it is a **level feature** (sensitive to vocabulary/character frequency shifts) and should exhibit **H₂ drift** with depth. This prediction is registered before plan_011 execution as an out-of-sample test of the level/shape framework.

**RC2 — "Does this generalize beyond Pythia?"**: MVP used same-family models (Pythia-2.8B generator + Pythia-410M reference). → Cross-family experiments: Qwen/OLMo generators + non-Pythia reference models (RQ1 cross-generator evaluation).

**RC3 — "Is 3-class sufficient? Why not finer-grained?"**: Attractor theory bounds paraphrasing to ~3 classes. → Secondary analysis: finer-grained ordinal classification (gen-0 through gen-4) on non-paraphrastic chains to test if more depth signal exists.

**RC4 — "How realistic are single-model chains?"**: Real web contamination involves diverse generators. → Cross-model chains (different generator per depth step) as primary evaluation setting (RQ3).

**RC5 — "What about human editing / post-processing?"**: Real-world synthetic text is often edited. → Robustness test with simulated human edits (random word replacement as lower-bound + LLM-simulated editing).

**RC6 — "Ecological validity — continuation vs real web content"**: Lab-constructed chains may not match wild distribution. → Multi-domain seeds (news, Wikipedia, scientific, creative) + multiple prompt types (continuation, elaboration, inspired rewriting).

**RC8 — "Aren't these just OOD detection features?"**: Reference-model entropy statistics are functionally NLL-based OOD scores (same signal backbone as DetectGPT/GLTR/Binoculars). Our contribution is NOT the features themselves but: (a) the problem formulation (ordinal depth estimation, not binary detection), (b) the empirical discovery that these features exhibit dual dynamics (level drift vs shape stationarity) under recursive generation, and (c) the practical application to risk-stratified data curation. Paper must explicitly connect to OOD detection + perplexity-based detection literature and position the contribution as primarily empirical/conceptual rather than methodological.

**RC9 — "Only ≤2.8B generators — does this transfer to frontier scale?"**: **Answered (plan-014, D011).** Qwen3-8B (7.6B params) added as 6th generator. Depth signal IS present at 8B scale — all feature-depth Spearman correlations significant. Cross-scale transfer gap: 8B held-out F1=0.69 vs ≤2.8B 0.76-0.85. P0-B volume-matched control: adding Qwen3-8B's +1.1pp improvement is 94% from generator diversity, not data volume. **Paper framing**: depth signal universality supported; cross-scale gap is honest limitation; scope narrowed to base models (see N3/N4 fixes).

**RC10 — "Text length confound"**: Hapax ratio and TTR are mechanically length-dependent. If generation chains produce texts of systematically different lengths, surface features may track length artifacts rather than distributional drift. → Length distribution analysis + length-normalized features + length-matched comparison (plan_013). Critical confound control.

**RC11 — "Downstream utility — single run, no CIs"**: Depth-aware filtering advantage must be validated with multiple seeds + bootstrap CIs + sample-count-matched comparison (to control for data size confound). Must use non-Pythia model for downstream fine-tuning (OLMo-1B) to avoid reference model circularity (Pythia-410M as both feature extractor and eval model).

## Contribution Positioning (D006+D007)
The contribution is **primarily empirical and conceptual**, not methodological:
1. **Problem formulation**: Ordinal depth estimation as a new task beyond binary detection (genuinely novel — no prior work)
2. **Empirical characterization**: Differential depth response across 6 generators / 3 families (including 7B+ scale), with robust cross-generator generalization (binary LOGO F1=0.723, 3-class LOGO F1=0.789). Scale-invariant phenomenon with honest cross-scale transfer gap.
3. **Negative finding**: Depth-aware data curation does NOT improve downstream CLM quality — depth fingerprinting is diagnostic, not curative (D009).

**Framing discipline (D007 — re-dream consensus):**
- Do NOT call the drift/stationarity split a "discovery" — it follows from location-shift properties of the NLL distribution (means shift under distributional drift, shapes don't). Acknowledge this explicitly.
- Do NOT use H1/H2 terminology (overloads time-series unit-root convention). Use "drifting" vs "stationary" or "differential response."
- Do NOT overclaim "dual dynamics" as a novel theoretical framework. Use "differential depth response" — more calibrated.
- Consider renaming "distributional fingerprinting" → "distributional depth profiling" (fingerprinting implies source identification, creates confusion with LLM attribution literature).
- Provide at least a speculative theoretical motivation for WHY shape features remain stationary (e.g., "shape is determined by sampling mechanism and architecture, invariant to input content drift").
- Report **realistic performance range** (0.68–0.86 per-generator held-out F1, binary LOGO F1=0.72, 3-class LOGO F1=0.79 with gen-0 caveat) in abstract/conclusion, not just best-case. **禁止用 CI width 作为 cross-generator 一致性论据**（Round 2 C1 critical）——用 per-gen F1 std/range 替代。
- R² on 5 aggregated depth means is statistically meaningless (3 df). Use individual-level Spearman ρ with bootstrap CIs throughout.

Related work must expand to 30+ references covering: perplexity-based detection (DetectGPT, GLTR, DNA-GPT, Binoculars), model collapse theory (Alemohammad et al., Dohmatob et al., Gerstgrasser et al., Guo et al.), OOD detection (Hendrycks & Gimpel), data quality scoring (DSIR, QuRating, CCNet), watermarking (Kirchenbauer et al.), vocabulary diversity (Guo et al. 2024, Padmakumar & He 2024, Holtzman et al. 2020), **stylometry/authorship attribution** (Stamatatos 2009, Koppel et al. 2009 — feature set is essentially stylometric), **iterative generation** (LLM as Broken Telephone ACL 2025, Markovian Generation Chains), **membership inference** (Shi et al. 2024).

## Venue Fit
- **EMNLP 2026**: Excellent fit — directly addresses "New Missions for NLP Research" theme (data contamination, synthetic data feedback loops, data governance). NLP-native venue. Empirical/conceptual contributions well-received. Novel task formulation + honest negative finding valued.

## Open Questions (pending P1-C)
- Instruct model depth response: if Qwen3-1.7B-Instruct shows drift → extend to 1-2 more instruct models; if not → limitation paragraph (scope narrowing already in place)
- Rd2-W4 (no validated alternative application): diagnostic framing is current defense; no new experiment planned unless P1-C opens a new angle

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All six generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects, enabling controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.764 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 under the 7-generator split; base-only yields 0.824, Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}).
Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
Extending depth fingerprinting to instruct models requires addressing these confounds---length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping---that instruction tuning introduces.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale, but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap (held-out F1\,=\,0.683 vs.\ 0.76--0.86 for $\leq$2.8B generators).
Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains show strongest drift (within-type F1\,=\,0.781) compared to elaboration (0.730), rewriting (0.737), and paraphrastic chains (binary F1\,=\,0.671 vs.\ 0.749 for continuation).
DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.809, binary F1\,=\,0.764), though the six generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
All seed texts are English Wikipedia excerpts; generalization to other languages and domains remains untested.

Our default analysis uses fixed decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$). A sampling ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}) shows robustness to moderate variation ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$, ${\leq}0.3$\,pp) but substantial degradation at $t{=}1.0$ ($-6$\,pp), indicating that depth fingerprinting assumes standard decoding regimes.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}) yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the practical resolution limit.

1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{Shape stationarity: mechanistic hypothesis.}
5	Distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
6	We hypothesize that this reflects a decomposition of the autoregressive generation process: at each token position, the output distribution is determined jointly by model parameters (fixed) and conditioning context (varying).
7	Recursive generation progressively shifts context toward the model's high-probability regions---reducing entropy mean---but does not alter the softmax architecture or sampling hyperparameters that determine distributional shape.
8	This predicts that shape features should remain stationary until generation depth reaches the model's fixed-point distribution, a regime not yet observed in our chain lengths ($\leq$4 steps).
9	Sampling ablation is consistent with this account: depth signal is robust to moderate temperature variation (${\leq}0.3$\,pp for $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$) but degrades substantially at $t = 1.0$ ($-6$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), where the sampling mechanism itself becomes the dominant source of distributional shape variation, overwhelming the depth signal.
10	
11	\paragraph{Prompt-type dependence.}
12	Differential depth response strength varies substantially across prompt types.
13	Continuation chains exhibit 16.9\% depth retention loss by gen-4, while elaboration chains retain 98.6\% of samples (Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
14	The 7-feature ensemble achieves within-type CV F1 of 0.781 for continuation vs.\ 0.730 for elaboration; cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal despite differing drift magnitudes.
15	These results bound depth fingerprinting's applicability: in near-paraphrastic settings (elaboration, rewriting), distributional drift attenuates more rapidly, consistent with semantic-preservation constraints acting as an anchor against distributional shift \cite{broken_telephone}.
16	
17	\paragraph{Corpus-level vs.\ document-level utility.}
18	The practical value of depth estimation depends on the unit of analysis.
19	At the individual document level, gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.64 implies a 36\% misclassification rate---insufficient for automated filtering but suitable for flagging suspect documents for human review.
20	At the corpus level, aggregate depth composition can be estimated with substantially lower error: over $n$ documents, estimation error scales as $O(1/\sqrt{n})$, making corpus-level provenance characterization reliable even with moderate per-document accuracy.
21	The 3-class design explicitly targets the most informative boundaries: human vs.\ machine (gen-0 vs.\ gen-1+) and shallow vs.\ deep recursion (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), where the distributional distinction is most actionable.
22	
23	\paragraph{Relation to model collapse.}
24	Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
25	Model collapse describes distributional degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs; we observe analogous drift---monotonic decrease in vocabulary diversity, compression of perplexity---in \emph{inference chains} without parameter updates.
26	Quantitatively, the magnitude differs: hapax ratio declines ${\sim}$14\% across 4 inference-chain depths, compared to catastrophic diversity loss reported after 5--10 retraining generations \cite{curse_of_recursion}.
27	We hypothesize that inference-chain drift represents an early, reversible stage of the same distributional narrowing process that becomes irreversible only when gradient updates amplify the shift.
28	This suggests depth fingerprinting features could serve as leading indicators: text exhibiting inference-chain drift signatures would, if recycled into training, accelerate the collapse regime.
29	Topic drift mediates rather than confounds this process: semantic narrowing accounts for less than 9\% of feature variance (maximum $R^2 = 0.082$ for entropy\_mean), and shape features are near-independent of semantic drift ($|\rho| = 0.068$).

\section{Discussion}

Distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
We hypothesize that this reflects a decomposition of the autoregressive generation process: at each token position, the output distribution is determined jointly by model parameters (fixed) and conditioning context (varying).
Recursive generation progressively shifts context toward the model's high-probability regions---reducing entropy mean---but does not alter the softmax architecture or sampling hyperparameters that determine distributional shape.
This predicts that shape features should remain stationary until generation depth reaches the model's fixed-point distribution, a regime not yet observed in our chain lengths ($\leq$4 steps).
Sampling ablation is consistent with this account: depth signal is robust to moderate temperature variation (${\leq}0.3$\,pp for $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$) but degrades substantially at $t = 1.0$ ($-6$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), where the sampling mechanism itself becomes the dominant source of distributional shape variation, overwhelming the depth signal.

\paragraph{Prompt-type dependence.}

Continuation chains exhibit 16.9\% depth retention loss by gen-4, while elaboration chains retain 98.6\% of samples (Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related}
3	
4	\subsection{AI-Generated Text Detection}
5	\label{sec:related-detection}
6	
7	Methods for distinguishing human-written from machine-generated text have evolved from statistical tests \cite{gltr,grover,release_strategies} to zero-shot reference-model approaches \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,dna_gpt} and learned classifiers \cite{feat_aug_transformer,reliable_detection,ld_score}.
8	Recent work pursues diverse signals including intrinsic dimensionality \cite{intrinsic_dimension}, surprisal diversity \cite{diveye}, and distributional gap measures \cite{generator_barrier}; see \citet{wu_survey_2025} and \citet{jawahar_survey} for surveys.
9	A persistent limitation is that these methods produce binary (real vs.\ synthetic) decisions.
10	Recent multi-class extensions---role recognition in human-LLM collaboration \cite{beyond_binary} and multi-generator attribution \cite{semeval2024_task8}---discriminate among different \emph{sources} rather than recursive generation \emph{depth}.
11	Even when detection scores correlate with depth, they exhibit high cross-generator variance as ordinal predictors (binary F1 from 0.52 to 0.71; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}), because each captures a single distributional property that generalizes inconsistently \cite{paraphrase_evades,detection_possibilities}.
12	Our contribution is not a new detection method but the task formulation (ordinal depth estimation) and the finding that combining drifting and stationary features yields consistent cross-generator performance.
13	
14	\paragraph{Source attribution vs.\ depth estimation.}
15	Source attribution identifies \emph{which} model generated a text \cite{uchendu_attribution,munir_looking_glass}; depth estimation answers \emph{how many recursive steps} produced it.
16	The two tasks are orthogonal, and our LOGO evaluation decouples generator identity from depth by holding out entire generators.
17	
18	\subsection{Model Collapse and Iterative Generation}
19	\label{sec:related-collapse}
20	
21	Self-consuming generative models progressively lose distributional coverage \cite{self_consuming_mad}, and model collapse is inevitable without fresh human data \cite{curse_of_recursion}, though careful data mixing can mitigate this \cite{model_collapse_avoidable,strong_model_collapse}.
22	These studies focus on \emph{training-loop} degradation; our setting studies \emph{inference chains}, where a fixed model generates text conditioned on its own prior output without retraining.
23	
24	Two concurrent works are most directly relevant.
25	\citet{broken_telephone} analyze paraphrasing and translation chains, showing progressive information loss.
26	\citet{markovian_chains} demonstrate that semantic-preservation constraints induce attractor dynamics bounding distinguishable depth to approximately three classes.
27	We differ in studying \emph{non-paraphrastic continuation} chains, where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal, and in focusing on \emph{estimating} depth rather than characterizing convergence.
28	
29	\subsection{Vocabulary Diversity and Stylometry}
30	\label{sec:related-diversity}
31	
32	Declining lexical diversity in LLM-generated text is documented in both training \cite{curious_decline} and deployment \cite{writing_diversity} settings.
33	Our surface features---TTR and hapax ratio---are classical stylometric measures \cite{stamatatos_survey,koppel_authorship} that we apply to inference chains, showing monotonic diversity decline across depths without model retraining.
34	We push beyond generator identity \cite{uchendu_attribution} to the \emph{depth} dimension, and show that diversity declines monotonically even under top-$p$ sampling \cite{nucleus_sampling}.
35	
36	\subsection{Data Quality and Provenance}
37	\label{sec:related-provenance}
38	
39	Scalable data curation relies on quality signals: distribution matching \cite{dsir}, LLM-based scoring \cite{qurating}, and perplexity filtering \cite{ccnet}, as demonstrated by large-scale efforts such as FineWeb \cite{fineweb} and Dolma \cite{dolma}.
40	Generation depth is a complementary provenance signal characterizing \emph{how many steps removed} text is from a human source.
41	
42	Proactive provenance through watermarking \cite{watermark_llm,synthid_text,aaronson_watermark} embeds identifiable patterns during generation, but watermark strength decays across multi-step chains \cite{chainwash}, motivating passive post-hoc methods.
43	Our depth fingerprinting operates on text alone without generator cooperation.
44	At the feature level, our NLL analysis connects to \citet{min_k_percent}, who use the probability tail for membership inference; we analyze the full NLL distribution for ordinal depth estimation.

1	\section{Results}
2	\label{sec:results}
3	
4	We evaluate depth fingerprinting along four axes: cross-generator classification (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}), differential depth response of individual features (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}), comparison with existing detection baselines (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), and downstream utility for data curation (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
5	
6	\subsection{Depth Classification Performance}
7	\label{sec:results-classification}
8	
9	Table~\ref{tab:logo-results} reports leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) macro-F1 for 3-class depth estimation (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) across six generators spanning three model families and parameter counts from 0.6B to 8.2B.
10	
11	The 7-feature ensemble achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.789 (Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}). Because gen-0 seed texts are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), the gen-0 class F1 (0.94) may be inflated; we therefore report a leak-free binary evaluation (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, F1\,=\,0.723) as the primary metric.
12	Per-generator binary F1 ranges from 0.641 (Qwen3-8B) to 0.795 (Pythia-1B); 3-class F1 ranges from 0.683 to 0.856.
13	Per-class F1 varies by depth: gen-0\,=\,0.94, gen-2+\,=\,0.80, gen-1\,=\,0.64; the primary difficulty lies in distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, where feature margins narrow.
14	
15	\paragraph{Cross-scale transfer.}
16	The six-generator evaluation includes Qwen3-8B (8.2B parameters), confirming that depth signal persists beyond the $\leq$2.8B training generators, though with a moderate gap: Qwen3-8B binary F1\,=\,0.641 (CI [0.625, 0.657]) vs.\ 0.68--0.80 for smaller generators.
17	Adding Qwen3-8B data improves classification on the original five generators (+0.8\,pp to 0.810); a volume-matched control confirms 94\% of this gain is attributable to generator diversity rather than data quantity.
18	
19	\paragraph{Cross-family generalization.}
20	Leave-one-family-out (LOFO) evaluation---holding out an entire model family and training on the remaining two---yields macro-F1 of 0.772 (Pythia held out), 0.762 (OLMo held out), and 0.754 (Qwen held out), confirming that depth features transfer across architectural families with only modest degradation (average $\Delta$\,=\,$-$2.6\,pp vs.\ LOGO).
21	
22	\paragraph{Cross-model chains.}
23	Cross-model chains---where each generation step uses a randomly selected generator---yield 3-class F1\,=\,0.809 and binary F1\,=\,0.764 under 5-fold stratified cross-validation, confirming that depth signal persists under generator heterogeneity.
24	
25	\paragraph{Length confound control.}
26	Text length correlates weakly with depth (Spearman $|\rho| < 0.14$).
27	Length-normalized feature trends are preserved, and length-matched subsampling yields comparable or higher F1 ($\Delta$\,=\,+0.041), ruling out length as a confound (Appendix~\ref{app:length}).
28	
29

32	\small

57	\subsection{Differential Depth Response}
58	\label{sec:results-differential}
59	
60	Features exhibit \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity measures drift monotonically with depth, while distributional shape measures remain near-stationary.

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	Web-crawled corpora increasingly contain LLM-generated text---estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}---and this proportion grows as generated text re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation.
5	The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text.
6	Understanding the distributional properties of such recursive generation is a prerequisite for characterizing text provenance, yet the phenomenon itself---how distributional features evolve across generation depths---remains underexplored.
7	
8	We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic generation chains under controlled conditions, using six base (pretrained) models from three families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen) spanning multiple scales.
9	We restrict to base models as a deliberate design choice: instruction-tuning introduces confounds---output length variability, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping---that obscure the generation mechanism's intrinsic behavior.
10	Preliminary experiments confirm this concern: instruct models show substantially degraded depth signal (\S\ref{sec:discussion}), motivating the controlled base-model setting as the appropriate starting point for isolating recursive drift phenomena.
11	
12	Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt}, like classical out-of-distribution methods \cite{ood_baseline,energy_ood,mahalanobis_ood}, provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, conflating qualitatively different material.
13	A first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties; deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.
14	We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}---classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label---and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora increasingly contain LLM-generated text---estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}---and this proportion grows as generated text re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text.
Understanding the distributional properties of such recursive generation is a prerequisite for characterizing text provenance, yet the phenomenon itself---how distributional features evolve across generation depths---remains underexplored.

We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic generation chains under controlled conditions, using six base (pretrained) models from three families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen) spanning multiple scales.
We restrict to base models as a deliberate design choice: instruction-tuning introduces confounds---output length variability, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping---that obscure the generation mechanism's intrinsic behavior.
Preliminary experiments confirm this concern: instruct models show substantially degraded depth signal (\S\ref{sec:discussion}), motivating the controlled base-model setting as the appropriate starting point for isolating recursive drift phenomena.

Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt}, like classical out-of-distribution methods \cite{ood_baseline,energy_ood,mahalanobis_ood}, provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, conflating qualitatively different material.
A first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties; deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.
We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}---classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label---and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores exhibit high cross-generator variance (binary F1 from 0.52 to 0.81; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), making any single detector unreliable.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence under semantic-preservation constraints; we study non-paraphrastic chains where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.

We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
We hypothesize that recursive generation induces a location shift in the NLL distribution while preserving its functional form; under this account, the sampling mechanism governs distributional shape regardless of input content.
The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723 for leak-free depth discrimination (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+).
However, the strength of this signal is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains exhibit stronger drift than elaboration or rewriting chains (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

We additionally report a negative finding: despite the effectiveness of quality-based data curation for pretraining \cite{fineweb,dolma}, depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling at equal sample count (perplexity: 2.367 vs.\ 2.387).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for characterizing how distributional properties evolve across recursive generation depths.
    \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We document differential depth response across six base-model generators spanning three model families: a 7-feature ensemble combining drifting and stationary features achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723 for leak-free depth discrimination, outperforming all individual detection baselines ($p < 0.001$).
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:related} surveys related work on text detection, model collapse, and data quality.
\S\ref{sec:method} describes generation chain construction, feature extraction, and evaluation protocol.
\S\ref{sec:results} presents classification results, differential depth response analysis, and baseline comparisons.
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses mechanistic hypotheses and scope boundaries.

6	Understanding the distributional properties of such recursive generation is a prerequisite for characterizing text provenance, yet the phenomenon itself---how distributional features evolve across generation depths---remains underexplored.
7	
8	We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic generation chains under controlled conditions, using six base (pretrained) models from three families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen) spanning multiple scales.
9	We restrict to base models as a deliberate design choice: instruction-tuning introduces confounds---output length variability, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping---that obscure the generation mechanism's intrinsic behavior.
10	Preliminary experiments confirm this concern: instruct models show substantially degraded depth signal (\S\ref{sec:discussion}), motivating the controlled base-model setting as the appropriate starting point for isolating recursive drift phenomena.
11	
12	Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt}, like classical out-of-distribution methods \cite{ood_baseline,energy_ood,mahalanobis_ood}, provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, conflating qualitatively different material.
13	A first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties; deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.
14	We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}---classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label---and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
15	No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
16	When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores exhibit high cross-generator variance (binary F1 from 0.52 to 0.81; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), making any single detector unreliable.
17	Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence under semantic-preservation constraints; we study non-paraphrastic chains where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.
18	
19	We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
20	We hypothesize that recursive generation induces a location shift in the NLL distribution while preserving its functional form; under this account, the sampling mechanism governs distributional shape regardless of input content.

We restrict to base models as a deliberate design choice: instruction-tuning introduces confounds---output length variability, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping---that obscure the generation mechanism's intrinsic behavior.
Preliminary experiments confirm this concern: instruct models show substantially degraded depth signal (\S\ref{sec:discussion}), motivating the controlled base-model setting as the appropriate starting point for isolating recursive drift phenomena.

Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt}, like classical out-of-distribution methods \cite{ood_baseline,energy_ood,mahalanobis_ood}, provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, conflating qualitatively different material.
A first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties; deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.
We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}---classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label---and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores exhibit high cross-generator variance (binary F1 from 0.52 to 0.81; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), making any single detector unreliable.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence under semantic-preservation constraints; we study non-paraphrastic chains where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.

We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
We hypothesize that recursive generation induces a location shift in the NLL distribution while preserving its functional form; under this account, the sampling mechanism governs distributional shape regardless of input content.
The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723 for leak-free depth discrimination (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+).
However, the strength of this signal is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains exhibit stronger drift than elaboration or rewriting chains (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

We additionally report a negative finding: despite the effectiveness of quality-based data curation for pretraining \cite{fineweb,dolma}, depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling at equal sample count (perplexity: 2.367 vs.\ 2.387).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for characterizing how distributional properties evolve across recursive generation depths.
    \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We document differential depth response across six base-model generators spanning three model families: a 7-feature ensemble combining drifting and stationary features achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723 for leak-free depth discrimination, outperforming all individual detection baselines ($p < 0.001$).
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:related} surveys related work on text detection, model collapse, and data quality.
\S\ref{sec:method} describes generation chain construction, feature extraction, and evaluation protocol.
\S\ref{sec:results} presents classification results, differential depth response analysis, and baseline comparisons.
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses mechanistic hypotheses and scope boundaries.

2	\label{sec:related}
3	
4	\subsection{AI-Generated Text Detection}
5	\label{sec:related-detection}
6	
7	Methods for distinguishing human-written from machine-generated text have evolved from statistical tests \cite{gltr,grover,release_strategies} to zero-shot reference-model approaches \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,dna_gpt} and learned classifiers \cite{feat_aug_transformer,reliable_detection,ld_score}.
8	Recent work pursues diverse signals including intrinsic dimensionality \cite{intrinsic_dimension}, surprisal diversity \cite{diveye}, and distributional gap measures \cite{generator_barrier}; see \citet{wu_survey_2025} and \citet{jawahar_survey} for surveys.
9	A persistent limitation is that these methods produce binary (real vs.\ synthetic) decisions.
10	Recent multi-class extensions---role recognition in human-LLM collaboration \cite{beyond_binary} and multi-generator attribution \cite{semeval2024_task8}---discriminate among different \emph{sources} rather than recursive generation \emph{depth}.
11	Even when detection scores correlate with depth, they exhibit high cross-generator variance as ordinal predictors (binary F1 from 0.52 to 0.71; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}), because each captures a single distributional property that generalizes inconsistently \cite{paraphrase_evades,detection_possibilities}.
12	Our contribution is not a new detection method but the task formulation (ordinal depth estimation) and the finding that combining drifting and stationary features yields consistent cross-generator performance.
13	
14	\paragraph{Source attribution vs.\ depth estimation.}
15	Source attribution identifies \emph{which} model generated a text \cite{uchendu_attribution,munir_looking_glass}; depth estimation answers \emph{how many recursive steps} produced it.
16	The two tasks are orthogonal, and our LOGO evaluation decouples generator identity from depth by holding out entire generators.
17	
18	\subsection{Model Collapse and Iterative Generation}
19	\label{sec:related-collapse}
20	
21	Self-consuming generative models progressively lose distributional coverage \cite{self_consuming_mad}, and model collapse is inevitable without fresh human data \cite{curse_of_recursion}, though careful data mixing can mitigate this \cite{model_collapse_avoidable,strong_model_collapse}.
22	These studies focus on \emph{training-loop} degradation; our setting studies \emph{inference chains}, where a fixed model generates text conditioned on its own prior output without retraining.
23	
24	Two concurrent works are most directly relevant.
25	\citet{broken_telephone} analyze paraphrasing and translation chains, showing progressive information loss.
26	\citet{markovian_chains} demonstrate that semantic-preservation constraints induce attractor dynamics bounding distinguishable depth to approximately three classes.
27	We differ in studying \emph{non-paraphrastic continuation} chains, where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal, and in focusing on \emph{estimating} depth rather than characterizing convergence.
28	
29	\subsection{Vocabulary Diversity and Stylometry}
30	\label{sec:related-diversity}
31	
32	Declining lexical diversity in LLM-generated text is documented in both training \cite{curious_decline} and deployment \cite{writing_diversity} settings.
33	Our surface features---TTR and hapax ratio---are classical stylometric measures \cite{stamatatos_survey,koppel_authorship} that we apply to inference chains, showing monotonic diversity decline across depths without model retraining.
34	We push beyond generator identity \cite{uchendu_attribution} to the \emph{depth} dimension, and show that diversity declines monotonically even under top-$p$ sampling \cite{nucleus_sampling}.
35	
36	\subsection{Data Quality and Provenance}
37	\label{sec:related-provenance}
38	
39	Scalable data curation relies on quality signals: distribution matching \cite{dsir}, LLM-based scoring \cite{qurating}, and perplexity filtering \cite{ccnet}, as demonstrated by large-scale efforts such as FineWeb \cite{fineweb} and Dolma \cite{dolma}.
40	Generation depth is a complementary provenance signal characterizing \emph{how many steps removed} text is from a human source.
41	
42	Proactive provenance through watermarking \cite{watermark_llm,synthid_text,aaronson_watermark} embeds identifiable patterns during generation, but watermark strength decays across multi-step chains \cite{chainwash}, motivating passive post-hoc methods.
43	Our depth fingerprinting operates on text alone without generator cooperation.
44	At the feature level, our NLL analysis connects to \citet{min_k_percent}, who use the probability tail for membership inference; we analyze the full NLL distribution for ordinal depth estimation.

Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?
We fine-tune OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) and evaluate perplexity on a held-out test set (Table~\ref{tab:downstream}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrc}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Test PPL} \\
\midrule
All depths            & 12{,}299 & 2.335 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Size-matched (random) & 3{,}951  & 2.367 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0--1 only       & 3{,}951  & 2.387 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
Binary-filtered       & 3{,}951  & 2.389 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0 only          & 797      & 2.681 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Downstream fine-tuning perplexity (OLMo-2-0425-1B, mean $\pm$ std across 3 seeds). At equal sample count, random subsampling (2.367) outperforms depth-aware curation (depth 0--1: 2.387, binary-filtered: 2.389).}
\label{tab:downstream}
\end{table}

The results are unambiguous: data quantity dominates depth composition.
Training on all 12{,}299 samples yields the lowest perplexity (2.335).
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951), random subsampling (2.367, 95\% CI [2.367, 2.367]) \emph{outperforms} both depth-stratified selection (depth 0--1: 2.387, 95\% CI [2.387, 2.388]; $\Delta$\,=\,0.020, $p$\,=\,0.25 by paired permutation test) and binary detection filtering (2.389).
Cross-seed variance is below 0.001 across all variants; the permutation test is underpowered ($n$\,=\,3 seeds; $p$\,=\,0.25 is the minimum achievable $p$-value), but the ranking is stable across seeds.
The formal Cohen's $d$\,=\,40.2 for the random vs.\ depth-stratified comparison reflects the near-zero cross-seed variance (pooled std\,$< 0.001$), not a large practical effect; the absolute PPL difference is 0.020 on a baseline of 2.367.

Restricting training to human-only text (depth 0, $n$\,=\,797) produces a sharp perplexity increase to 2.681, driven primarily by the 5$\times$ reduction in data volume rather than depth composition per se.

Knowing the generation depth of a document does not, by itself, make it more or less useful for training.

\label{app:sampling-sensitivity}

\label{tab:sampling-ablation}
\small

\toprule

2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	Web-crawled corpora increasingly contain LLM-generated text---estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}---and this proportion grows as generated text re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation.
5	The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text.
6	Understanding the distributional properties of such recursive generation is a prerequisite for characterizing text provenance, yet the phenomenon itself---how distributional features evolve across generation depths---remains underexplored.
7	
8	We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic generation chains under controlled conditions, using six base (pretrained) models from three families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen) spanning multiple scales.
9	We restrict to base models as a deliberate design choice: instruction-tuning introduces confounds---output length variability, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping---that obscure the generation mechanism's intrinsic behavior.
10	Preliminary experiments confirm this concern: instruct models show substantially degraded depth signal (\S\ref{sec:discussion}), motivating the controlled base-model setting as the appropriate starting point for isolating recursive drift phenomena.
11	
12	Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt}, like classical out-of-distribution methods \cite{ood_baseline,energy_ood,mahalanobis_ood}, provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, conflating qualitatively different material.
13	A first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties; deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.
14	We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}---classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label---and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
15	No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
16	When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores exhibit high cross-generator variance (binary F1 from 0.52 to 0.81; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), making any single detector unreliable.
17	Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence under semantic-preservation constraints; we study non-paraphrastic chains where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.
18	
19	We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
20	We hypothesize that recursive generation induces a location shift in the NLL distribution while preserving its functional form; under this account, the sampling mechanism governs distributional shape regardless of input content.
21	The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723 for leak-free depth discrimination (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+).
22	However, the strength of this signal is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains exhibit stronger drift than elaboration or rewriting chains (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
23

The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text.
Understanding the distributional properties of such recursive generation is a prerequisite for characterizing text provenance, yet the phenomenon itself---how distributional features evolve across generation depths---remains underexplored.

We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic generation chains under controlled conditions, using six base (pretrained) models from three families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen) spanning multiple scales.
We restrict to base models as a deliberate design choice: instruction-tuning introduces confounds---output length variability, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping---that obscure the generation mechanism's intrinsic behavior.
Preliminary experiments confirm this concern: instruct models show substantially degraded depth signal (\S\ref{sec:discussion}), motivating the controlled base-model setting as the appropriate starting point for isolating recursive drift phenomena.

Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt}, like classical out-of-distribution methods \cite{ood_baseline,energy_ood,mahalanobis_ood}, provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, conflating qualitatively different material.
A first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties; deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.
We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}---classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label---and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores exhibit high cross-generator variance (binary F1 from 0.52 to 0.81; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), making any single detector unreliable.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence under semantic-preservation constraints; we study non-paraphrastic chains where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.

We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
We hypothesize that recursive generation induces a location shift in the NLL distribution while preserving its functional form; under this account, the sampling mechanism governs distributional shape regardless of input content.
The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723 for leak-free depth discrimination (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+).
However, the strength of this signal is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains exhibit stronger drift than elaboration or rewriting chains (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

We additionally report a negative finding: despite the effectiveness of quality-based data curation for pretraining \cite{fineweb,dolma}, depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling at equal sample count (perplexity: 2.367 vs.\ 2.387).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for characterizing how distributional properties evolve across recursive generation depths.
    \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We document differential depth response across six base-model generators spanning three model families: a 7-feature ensemble combining drifting and stationary features achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723 for leak-free depth discrimination, outperforming all individual detection baselines ($p < 0.001$).
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:related} surveys related work on text detection, model collapse, and data quality.
\S\ref{sec:method} describes generation chain construction, feature extraction, and evaluation protocol.
\S\ref{sec:results} presents classification results, differential depth response analysis, and baseline comparisons.
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses mechanistic hypotheses and scope boundaries.
